title: Taxonomically important characters may be useless products of correlated growth

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Taxonomically important characters may be useless products of correlated growth

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Structural differences that systematists treat as highly important, such as differences between outer and inner seeds of Umbelliferae, may arise entirely from unknown laws of correlated growth without being of any use to the species.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence we see that modifications of structure, viewed by systematists as of high value, may be wholly due to unknown laws of correlated growth, and without being, as far as we can see, of the slightest service to the species.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Correlation of growth.”. Scope: plants and animals; characters used in classification

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.46

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Selected cases can be investigated with developmental and fitness data, but Darwin's permissive 'may' claim has a weak refutation criterion. Existing datasets rarely combine diagnostic morphology, developmental covariance and fitness.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For taxonomically diagnostic structures, map developmental covariance, genetic architecture and measured fitness effects. A character arising as a correlated response with no detectable direct fitness effect supports the proposed possibility; consistent direct selection refutes it for that character.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Failure to detect utility does not establish that a character is useless.

Historical correlated response and later co-option are difficult to distinguish.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Developmental correlation and a near-zero selection gradient would favour a byproduct reading for a particular character, and fragments of those data exist. The wording only asserts that such characters may arise, so counterexamples do not refute it, and proving uselessness is biased toward the claim. Existing datasets support case studies, not a general decision.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For characters given high taxonomic weight, estimate their developmental correlation with other traits and the selection gradient on the character itself. A strong correlation together with a gradient indistinguishable from zero would support the possibility that the character is a useless byproduct; a consistently positive gradient would show that those particular characters are retained by selection, without closing a claim phrased as a possibility.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A possibility claim is confirmed by one solid case and is barely refutable.

Selection gradients on fine taxonomic characters are rarely measured.

Failure to find a function is weak evidence that a character is useless.
